lessons.title: Building a Time-Series Momentum Signal on Any Asset

body.text: A time-series momentum signal asks exactly one question of an asset: has it been going up or down against its own recent history? It never compares that asset to any other, which is precisely why the same formula can be pointed at Nifty, gold, a G-Sec future, and USD-INR without ever needing to ask whether those four things are even comparable to begin with.

children.text: Lesson 1 made the case for trend-following. This lesson builds the actual signal: how to measure trend, how to size a position once you have measured it, how to choose a look-back period, and how to avoid the single most common bug that quietly inflates every naive momentum backtest, look-ahead bias.
Time-Series Momentum: The Simplest Version of the Signal

markDefs.definition: A momentum signal based purely on an asset's own past return, independent of how any other asset has performed. Contrasts with cross-sectional momentum, which ranks assets against each other and is harder to apply meaningfully across genuinely different asset classes like equities, commodities, and currencies.

children.text: takes the sign of an asset's trailing return over some look-back window: go long if that trailing return is positive, go short if it is negative. It never asks how this asset's return compares to any other asset's return, which matters here specifically because ranking Nifty against gold against USD-INR the way a cross-sectional equity momentum strategy ranks stocks against each other would not be a meaningful comparison. Time-series momentum sidesteps that entirely by asking each asset only about itself.

body.caption: The basic time-series momentum signal: the sign of the asset's own trailing return over the N-period look-back window ending the prior period, +1 for long, -1 for short.

children.text: Position Sizing: Why Volatility Scaling Matters More Than Direction

A signal only tells you direction. Chapter 3's closing lesson already showed that equal notional sizing does not produce equal risk, and that problem shows up immediately here: sizing a Nifty position and a G-Sec futures position identically, using the same signal, would let Nifty's much higher volatility dominate the trend book's total risk, exactly the same imbalance Lesson 5 of Chapter 3 demonstrated with capital weights. The standard fix is volatility scaling: size each position inversely to its own recent volatility, so every trend bet targets roughly the same risk contribution rather than the same notional exposure.

body.caption: Volatility-scaled position size. Sigma_target is the desk's chosen risk level per position; sigma_asset,t is the asset's own recent realized volatility. Lower-volatility assets get a larger multiplier, higher-volatility assets a smaller one.
Illustrative Position Multipliers at a 10% Target Volatility

body.text: This is the exact same equal-risk logic from Chapter 3's closing lesson, applied at the individual position level rather than the whole-portfolio level. A vol-scaled trend book naturally sizes its G-Sec futures position more than three times larger, in multiplier terms, than its Nifty position, specifically to prevent Nifty's volatility from silently dominating the book's total risk.

children.text: Look-Back Period: The Trade-off Between Responsiveness and Reliability

Choosing N, the look-back window, is the same noise-versus-responsiveness trade-off Chapter 3's correlation lesson covered for rolling windows, applied here to trend measurement instead. A short look-back, a few weeks, reacts fast to a genuine new trend but generates far more false signals in a choppy, range-bound market, the exact whipsaw problem from Chapter 1's opening example. A long look-back, closer to a year, filters out more noise but reacts slowly and can hold a position well past when the trend it was originally following has actually ended. Most practitioners do not pick a single window; Lesson 4 covers combining several look-back horizons into one signal, precisely to avoid betting the whole strategy on one arbitrary window length.
Avoiding Look-Ahead Bias: A Concrete Implementation Checklist

The single most common bug in a homemade momentum backtest is including today's own return in the data used to decide today's position, which is impossible to replicate live, since you do not know today's return until the day is over. Both the trend signal and the volatility estimate used to size it must be computed using only data available strictly before the position is taken.

body.code:
import numpy as np

lookback = 252   # ~12 months of daily data
vol_window = 60
target_vol = 0.10  # 10% annualized

log_ret = np.log(prices / prices.shift(1))

# Signal: sign of the trailing lookback return, using only data
# available strictly before today. shift(1) is what prevents
# look-ahead bias here.
trailing_return = log_ret.rolling(lookback).sum().shift(1)
signal = np.sign(trailing_return)

# Position size: scale to a constant target volatility, using
# realized volatility estimated only from data available before today
realized_vol = log_ret.rolling(vol_window).std().shift(1) * np.sqrt(252)
position = signal * (target_vol / realized_vol)
body.caption: Both the signal and the volatility scaling use .shift(1), so today's position depends only on information that actually existed before today's trading began.

body.text: A backtest that accidentally includes today's return in either the trailing return calculation or the volatility estimate will look meaningfully better than the strategy can actually perform live, since it is effectively trading with foresight of the day's own outcome. This is one of the most common, and most quietly damaging, mistakes in systematic backtesting, alongside the survivorship bias trap covered in Chapter 2.

body.title: The Suspiciously High Sharpe Ratio
body.scenario: A junior quant researcher builds a time-series momentum backtest and reports a Sharpe ratio well above what any published trend-following track record typically shows. On review, their code computes the trailing return and realized volatility using a rolling window that includes today's own return, without any shift applied, before using that same day's signal to size that same day's position.
body.prompt: What specifically is wrong with this implementation, and why does it produce an unrealistically high Sharpe ratio?
body.modelAnswer: The backtest has a look-ahead bias bug: by including today's own return in both the trailing-return signal calculation and the volatility estimate, and then using that same day's signal to determine that same day's position, the strategy is effectively trading with knowledge of today's outcome before the day has actually happened. In live trading, today's return is not known until the trading day is over, so this exact sequence of decisions could never actually be executed in real time. The fix is to shift both the trailing return calculation and the volatility estimate by one period, so that any given day's position depends only on information that was genuinely available before that day's trading began, exactly as shown in this lesson's code example.

body.title: Computing a Position Multiplier
body.prompt: An asset has annualized volatility of 15%. Using a target volatility of 10%, what position size multiplier should be applied, using target_vol / asset_vol? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: 10 / 15 ≈ 0.67. This asset is more volatile than the 10% target, so it receives a multiplier below 1, a smaller position than a lower-volatility asset would get for the same signal, exactly the equal-risk logic from Chapter 3's closing lesson applied here.

body.title: Why Volatility Scaling, Not Equal Notional Sizing
body.question: Based on this lesson and Chapter 3's covariance work, why does a multi-asset trend system size positions inversely to each asset's volatility rather than giving every asset the same notional position size?
options: Because volatility scaling guarantees the strategy will never lose money
Because equal notional sizing would let the highest-volatility assets dominate the book's total risk, exactly the equal-weight-is-not-equal-risk problem Chapter 3 demonstrated
Because regulators require volatility scaling for all systematic strategies
Because lower-volatility assets always produce higher returns
body.explanation: Volatility scaling exists to prevent exactly the imbalance Chapter 3's closing lesson demonstrated with capital weights: without it, a high-volatility asset like Nifty would contribute a disproportionate share of the book's total risk relative to a low-volatility asset like G-Sec futures, even if both received the identical trend signal.

points: Time-series momentum asks only whether an asset's own trailing return is positive or negative, unlike cross-sectional momentum, which requires ranking assets against each other
Position sizing should scale inversely with an asset's own volatility, targeting equal risk contribution per bet rather than equal notional exposure

Look-back window choice carries the same noise-versus-responsiveness trade-off as Chapter 3's correlation windows: shorter windows react faster but whipsaw more, longer windows are smoother but slower
Both the trend signal and the volatility estimate used to size it must be computed using only data available strictly before the position is taken, using something like shift(1) in code
Look-ahead bias, accidentally using today's own return to decide today's position, is one of the most common and most damaging backtesting mistakes, alongside survivorship bias from Chapter 2
Lesson 3 applies this exact signal simultaneously to Nifty, Gold, and Crude as a concrete case study
